Two real, independent sources on this exact discipline agree, in their own words.
A frame's own width is how often it sat on the real stack; an allocator's own overhead is a real, measured, sometimes decisive share of the real cost.

So here's why a flamegraph earns its own shape: a call tree can be several real functions deep, and the one actually spending the real time is rarely sitting at the top where a casual glance would land.

That's also why profiling and benchmarking answer two genuinely different questions: a benchmark from the last chapter told you whether a change helped or hurt overall, while a profiler tells you exactly where, inside the real code, that cost is actually coming from.

And the allocator result matters for the identical reason the tail mattered last chapter: a cost that looks too small to bother with on average can still be the real, decisive share once you actually go measure it rather than assume it away.
